title: Carbohydrates. Structure and properties of monosaccharides. Di-, homo- and heteropolysaccharides

goals.text: To teach the student the main carbohydrates of food, the classification, stereoisomerism and cyclic forms of monosaccharides, their chemical properties (oxidation and reduction), their derivatives used in medicine, reducing and non-reducing disaccharides, and the structure and significance of homopolysaccharides and the heteropolysaccharides of connective tissue.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the classification of monosaccharides as aldoses/ketoses and by the number of carbons, the D/L series and epimers;
the pyranose and furanose forms, α- and β-anomers, and mutarotation;
the oxidation (aldonic and glucuronic acids) and reduction (sorbitol) of monosaccharides;
reducing (maltose, lactose, cellobiose) and non-reducing (sucrose, trehalose) disaccharides;
the structure of starch, glycogen, cellulose, chitin and pectin;
the significance of hyaluronic acid, chondroitin sulfates and heparin.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write the Fischer and Haworth formulas of glucose;
explain the detection of reducing carbohydrates by the Trommer and Fehling reactions;
determine the composition of a disaccharide and the type of glycosidic bond;
explain the chemical basis of disorders of carbohydrate metabolism (lactase deficiency, diabetes mellitus).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: A disaccharide is **reducing** if one of its monosaccharides still has a **free hemiacetal (glycosidic) hydroxyl** (maltose, lactose). In sucrose both anomeric hydroxyls are used up in the bond — it is **non-reducing**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Disaccharides: **“Mal-Glu-Glu, Lac-Gal-Glu, Suc-Glu-Fru”** — maltose = glucose + glucose, lactose = galactose + glucose, sucrose = glucose + fructose.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Humans have no enzyme that breaks down **cellulose** (β-1,4-glycosidase): it is not digested, but as **dietary fiber** it stimulates gut motility and binds cholesterol and bile acids. Starch, on the other hand, has α-1,4 bonds and is easily broken down by amylase.

blocks.text: **Carbohydrates** are polyhydroxycarbonyl compounds and their derivatives; most have the general formula C~n~(H~2~O)~m~. They provide ≈ 50–60 % of dietary energy and are the main energy source; the brain and red blood cells use almost only glucose.

head: Carbohydrate
Type
Source

items: **By the carbonyl group:** aldoses (aldehyde group — glucose, galactose, ribose) and ketoses (keto group — fructose, ribulose).
**By the number of carbons:** trioses (glyceraldehyde, dihydroxyacetone), tetroses, pentoses (ribose, deoxyribose, xylose), hexoses (glucose, galactose, mannose, fructose).
**The D and L series** are defined by the configuration of the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl group (C-5 in hexoses); natural monosaccharides belong mainly to the **D series**.

blocks.text: An aldohexose has 4 chiral carbons, so 2^4^ = 16 stereoisomers (8 pairs of enantiomers) exist. Diastereomers that differ at only one chiral center are called **epimers**: D-glucose and D-galactose are **C-4** epimers, D-glucose and D-mannose are **C-2** epimers.

In solution monosaccharides exist mainly in **cyclic** form: the carbonyl group forms an intramolecular hemiacetal with a hydroxyl of the same molecule. A six-membered ring is a **pyranose**, a five-membered one a **furanose**. The new chiral center that appears when the ring closes (C-1) is the **anomeric** center: OH below the plane of the ring (in the Haworth formula) — the **α**-anomer, above — the **β**-anomer.

blocks.label: Figure 12.1
blocks.caption: The α- and β-pyranose forms of D-glucose (Haworth projection): they differ only in the position of the hydroxyl at C-1 and interconvert in solution through the open form (diagram).

blocks.text: **Mutarotation** is the change of the specific rotation of a freshly prepared solution with time until it reaches an equilibrium value: α-D-glucose (+112°) and β-D-glucose (+18.7°) interconvert in solution through the open form; at equilibrium ≈ 36 % α and 64 % β (+52.5°).

sections.title: 3. Chemical properties of monosaccharides. Oxidation and reduction

blocks.title: Table 12.2. Oxidation and reduction of glucose
head: Reaction
Product
Significance
rows: forms conjugates with bilirubin, drugs and toxins in the liver (detoxification)

blocks.text: **Reducing property:** aldoses (and ketoses in an alkaline medium) reduce alkaline Cu^2+^ solution: in the **Trommer** and **Fehling** reactions light blue Cu(OH)~2~ turns on heating into a brick-red precipitate of Cu~2~O; with **Tollens’** reagent a “silver mirror” forms.

items: **Amino sugars:** glucosamine, galactosamine (their N-acetyl derivatives are part of heteropolysaccharides); glucosamine is used as a chondroprotector in joint diseases.
**Deoxy sugars:** 2-deoxyribose — part of DNA.
**Ascorbic acid** (vitamin C) — a lactone derivative of glucose, a strong reducing agent; needed for collagen synthesis and iron absorption.
**Lactulose** (galactose + fructose) — a synthetic disaccharide not absorbed in the intestine: a laxative that reduces ammonia absorption in hepatic encephalopathy.

parts.text: In diabetes mellitus blood glucose combines non-enzymatically with the amino groups of proteins (**glycation**): glycated hemoglobin **HbA~1c~** reflects the mean glycemia over the last 2–3 months (normal < 5.7 %, in diabetes ≥ 6.5 %). Blood glucose is now measured by the glucose oxidase method; the Trommer and Fehling reactions are historical methods.

blocks.text: **Formation of maltose from starch:** salivary and pancreatic **α-amylase** hydrolyzes the internal α-1,4-glycosidic bonds of starch; maltose, maltotriose and α-dextrins are formed, and these are broken down to glucose in the intestine by **maltase** and isomaltase. In theory, maltose can be obtained from two molecules of α-D-glucopyranose by removing water (from the hydroxyls at C-1 of the first and C-4 of the second).

parts.text: **Lactase deficiency** (lactose intolerance): lactose is not broken down in the small intestine, passes into the large intestine and is fermented by bacteria — bloating, pain and diarrhea. In most adults (especially in Asian peoples) lactase activity falls with age. Treatment: lactose-free milk, fermented dairy products, lactase preparations.

parts.text: The heavy branching of glycogen gives it many “ends”: glycogen phosphorylase can release glucose from many ends at once, quickly supplying blood glucose (liver) or muscle work (muscle).

blocks.text: Each glucose residue of cellulose has three free OH groups; they form esters with acids.

items: **Cellulose acetates** (with acetic anhydride): acetate rayon, films, formerly hemodialysis membranes; tablet coatings (cellulose acetate phthalate — an enteric coating).

**Cellulose nitrates** (with nitric acid): the lightly nitrated form is **pyroxylin (colloxylin)**; its solution in ether–alcohol is **collodion**, used as a sealing coat for small wounds and surgical sutures. The fully nitrated form is explosive guncotton.
**Methyl- and carboxymethylcellulose** — thickeners and artificial tears in eye drops, ointments and tablets.

blocks.text: **Glycosaminoglycans** (mucopolysaccharides) are heteropolysaccharides built from repeating disaccharide units (uronic acid + amino sugar) and strongly negatively charged because of their sulfate and carboxyl groups. They bind a lot of water and form the gel medium of connective tissue.

blocks.title: Table 12.5. The main glycosaminoglycans
head: Substance
Disaccharide unit
Location and function
rows: synovial fluid, vitreous body, skin; lubrication, shock absorption
mast cells; an **anticoagulant** — activates antithrombin III

parts.text: **Heparin** is the most negatively charged biomolecule; it binds to antithrombin III and rapidly inactivates thrombin and factor Xa — it is used to treat thrombosis and embolism; its antidote is the positively charged **protamine sulfate**. When lysosomal enzymes are deficient, glycosaminoglycans accumulate and hereditary **mucopolysaccharidoses** (Hurler and Hunter syndromes) develop.

skills.title: Skill: detecting reducing carbohydrates (the Trommer reaction)

items: Put 1 mL of carbohydrate solution and 1 mL of 10 % NaOH into a test tube.
Add 5 % CuSO~4~ dropwise — the Cu(OH)~2~ that first forms dissolves on shaking and a blue solution forms (a property of polyhydric alcohols).
Heat the upper part of the solution.
If the carbohydrate is reducing, a yellow CuOH and then a brick-red Cu~2~O precipitate forms.
With sucrose the reaction is negative; if you first hydrolyze it with acid and test again, it is positive.

skills.title: Skill: analyzing the formula of a disaccharide

items: Identify the two monosaccharide residues in the molecule (pyranose or furanose; glucose, galactose or fructose).
Find the carbons that form the glycosidic bond (1→4, 1→2, 1→1).
Determine the anomeric configuration of the bond (α or β).
Check whether a free hemiacetal OH is present — if so, the sugar is reducing.
Name the disaccharide and say which enzyme breaks it down.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A 22-year-old student complains of bloating, pain and loose stools 1–2 hours after drinking milk. He tolerates kefir and cheese well.
cases.ask: What is the condition? Explain the chemical mechanism.
cases.answer: **Lactase deficiency** (lactose intolerance). Lactose is a disaccharide of galactose and glucose with a β-1,4-glycosidic bond; it is broken down by **lactase** (β-galactosidase) of the small intestinal mucosa. When the enzyme is lacking, lactose is not absorbed; being osmotically active, it draws water into the intestine (diarrhea), and in the large intestine bacteria ferment it into gases (H~2~, CO~2~, CH~4~) and acids (bloating, pain). In kefir and cheese lactose has been partly broken down by bacteria, so they are well tolerated.

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: A patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus has fasting glucose of 8.2 mmol/L and HbA~1c~ = 8.5 %.
cases.ask: How is HbA~1c~ formed and what does it show? Which property of carbohydrates is involved?
cases.answer: The open (aldehyde) form of glucose condenses non-enzymatically with the amino group of the N-terminal valine of the hemoglobin β-chain (Schiff base → Amadori rearrangement) — **glycated hemoglobin** is formed. The reaction depends on blood glucose concentration and time, and since red cells live ≈ 120 days, HbA~1c~ reflects the mean glycemia over the last 2–3 months. 8.5 % means the diabetes is poorly controlled (the target is usually < 7 %); treatment should be adjusted.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A patient with deep vein thrombosis was given heparin. A few hours later signs of bleeding appeared.
cases.ask: Explain the chemical structure and mechanism of action of heparin. How does the antidote act?
cases.answer: Heparin is a highly sulfated glycosaminoglycan built from glucosamine and uronic acids; it is the most strongly negatively charged biomolecule. Through a specific pentasaccharide sequence it binds to **antithrombin III** and increases a thousandfold the rate at which antithrombin inactivates thrombin and factor Xa — blood clotting slows. The antidote is the positively charged protein **protamine sulfate**: it forms an electrostatic complex with heparin and neutralizes it.

Stereoisomers that differ at one chiral center (glucose–galactose, C-4)
The α- and β-cyclic forms differing in the position of OH at C-1
Change of optical rotation in solution because the α- and β-anomers interconvert
Product of oxidation of glucose at C-6; conjugation (detoxification)
The highly branched (α-1,4 + α-1,6) storage polysaccharide of animals
β-1,4-glucan; not digested by humans — dietary fiber
A highly sulfated glycosaminoglycan; an anticoagulant via antithrombin III
